analysis.investment_thesis: Borosil Renewables is a capital-intensive solar glass manufacturer burning cash, posting back-to-back net losses (₹50 Cr in FY24, ₹87 Cr in FY25), with negative ROE of -8.9% — the precise opposite of the steady compounder I seek. At a meaningless P/E of 73x on a loss-making business, the market is pricing in a recovery that the financials give no reason to trust.
key_strengths: Promoter holding at 58.77% — reasonable skin in the game
Debt/Equity of 0.23 is within tolerable range after debt was partly paid down from ₹576 Cr peak in FY24 to ₹203 Cr in FY25
Revenue has grown from ₹156 Cr (2014) to ₹1,476 Cr (2025) — the business has scale
key_risks: Collapsed profitability: EBITDA fell from ₹256 Cr (FY22) to ₹73 Cr (FY25) even as revenue doubled — severe margin compression from Chinese solar glass pricing
Persistently negative free cash flow every year since FY18 (except marginally positive in FY25 at -₹8 Cr) — this business destroys cash
Earnings have no consistency: net profit swung from +₹166 Cr (FY22) to -₹87 Cr (FY25) — exactly the volatility I refuse to tolerate
red_flags: Negative ROE (-8.9%) and ROCE (-4.41%) — capital is being destroyed, not compounded
Historical 'profits' were largely illusory: in FY17, Other Income was ₹135 Cr vs Net Profit of ₹137 Cr — core operations contributed almost nothing
Borrowings surged from ₹114 Cr (FY19) to ₹576 Cr (FY24) to fund capex — aggressive debt-funded expansion with poor return on that capital
Sector entirely outside my circle of competence — solar glass is cyclical, commodity-like, and directly exposed to Chinese dumping
analysis.detailed_analysis:
This business fails my checklist at nearly every checkpoint. I built DMart by obsessing over return on capital — Borosil Renewables earns negative returns on both equity (-8.9%) and capital employed (-4.41%) while carrying a market cap of ₹6,987 Cr. The free cash flow has been negative in 4 of the last 5 years, and capex of ₹373 Cr, ₹348 Cr, ₹217 Cr in successive years produced EBITDA that collapsed from ₹256 Cr to ₹73 Cr. That is the definition of value-destroying capital allocation.

The 25.84% operating margin figure in the data appears to conflict with the actual income statement (₹58 Cr operating income on ₹1,476 Cr revenue = ~4% margin), suggesting it may reflect a different period or calculation — but it doesn't matter, because the company is loss-making regardless. The sector is structurally difficult: solar glass competes directly with heavily subsidised Chinese manufacturers, making durable pricing power nearly impossible. This is not a business I would own at any price, let alone at 73x earnings when there are no earnings.
